subtopic: Found money or a lost wallet
subtype: Approach: asking the police or shop counter to display a notice [Action]
passage: Come here and listen. When I was ten, I, your grandmother Shalini, was waiting at the bus stand with my mother's bundle when I saw a cloth bag under the bench. I peeked inside: bundles of notes. My knees turned to water. I did not touch it again. I ran to the chai seller, Ramu Kaka, and said, "Please phone the police post. Somebody must be missing this." Constable Hrithik came, wrote down what I said and took the bag, telling us that whoever came had to describe what was inside. Two days later a farmer came, weeping, and named every bundle. I never saw that money again, and I never missed it.

qa.q: Where did Shalini see the cloth bag?
qa.a: Shalini saw it under the bench at the bus stand.

qa.q: What did Shalini feel when the bundles of notes came into view?
qa.a: Shocked and scared, since Shalini's knees turned to water and Shalini did not touch the bag again.

qa.q: What choice at the bus stand made sure the money reached its owner?
qa.a: Shalini asked the chai seller to phone the police post, which held the bag until the right person could describe what was inside.

qa.q: How might the farmer have felt when the bag was returned?
qa.a: Relieved and overwhelmed, since the farmer came weeping and named every bundle.

grounding: A child finds a bag of cash and has the tea seller call the police post, which holds it for the owner to claim.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: splitting money into spend, save and give [Thinking]
passage:
First of the month. Indu received two hundred rupees and set three jars on the shelf. "One for a treat, one for the book I want, one for giving," she said. Eighty into the first, ninety into the second, thirty into the third.
Second Saturday. She took twenty from the treat jar for jalebis. Her cousin Vishal had lost his lunch money, so she dropped ten rupees from the giving jar into his hand.
Last day. The book jar held ninety, and the book cost more. Indu shrugged. Next month it would fit.

qa.q: How many jars did Indu use?
qa.a: Indu used three jars.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling as she saw the book jar was still short?
qa.a: Calm and patient, since she shrugged and knew it would fit the next month.

qa.q: What could Indu do if she wants the book sooner, and why?
qa.a: She could take a little more from the treat jar for a month or earn a few rupees with small jobs at home, so the book jar fills faster.

qa.q: How might Vishal have felt when Indu gave him the ten rupees?
qa.a: Grateful and relieved, since he had lost his lunch money.

grounding: A girl splits her monthly money into three jars for a treat, a book she wants and giving, and uses each for its purpose.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: saving for a specific goal [Action]
passage: The football in the shop window cost four hundred rupees. Kamal received fifty a week. He borrowed a pencil and did the sum on the back of his hand: eight weeks. He drew eight boxes on a chart above his bed and coloured one at the end of every week. On Fridays at the canteen, when the chips smelled so good, Kamal walked past with his hands in his pockets. His sister Aparna teased him. "Is your football made of chips?" In the eighth week he counted his coins into the shopkeeper's palm, and the ball rolled into his arms.

qa.q: How many weeks did Kamal need to save?
qa.a: He needed eight weeks.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling as he walked past the chips?
qa.a: Tempted but determined, since he kept his hands in his pockets and kept the football in mind.

qa.q: What could Kamal add to his plan for a surprise expense, and why?
qa.a: He could add a spare box or earn a little by helping at home, so one unexpected cost does not wreck the eight weeks.

qa.q: How does Aparna see Kamal's saving?
qa.a: Aparna finds it funny enough to tease him, though she seems to notice how seriously he keeps to it.

grounding: A boy works out how many weeks of pocket money a football needs, marks a chart and skips canteen chips.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: spending it all at once on impulse [Pitfall]
passage:
Sunday. Pocket money day! I bought two sticker sheets and a big bag of sweets straight away and passed them along the whole bench. Best day ever.
Friday of the second week. I looked in my tin. Nothing, not one coin. And tomorrow is Gopika's birthday. Amma said a small gift would be nice. All I have is an empty tin and stickers already stuck in my book. My face went hot at school when everyone talked about presents. I will give her a drawing, I guess. I hope she does not mind. - Pranav

qa.q: When did Pranav spend the pocket money?
qa.a: Pranav spent it straight away on pocket money day.

qa.q: How did Pranav feel at school when everyone talked about presents?
qa.a: Embarrassed, since Pranav's face went hot, having nothing left to buy a gift with.

qa.q: What could Pranav do differently next time, and why?
qa.a: Pranav could set aside a small part for surprises like birthdays before buying treats, so the tin is not empty by week two.

qa.q: How might Gopika feel about receiving a drawing?
qa.a: Gopika may be touched that it was made for her, though she might have expected a bought gift.

grounding: A child spends all the pocket money at once on stickers and sweets, and has nothing left for a friend's gift.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: comparing prices at different shops [Thinking]
passage: At the school store a notebook costs forty rupees. On the way home I saw the same notebook in the lane shop for thirty. "Ten rupees less," I said aloud, and Harish Uncle grinned. "Tell your friends too, beti." I did the sum: two notebooks here save twenty rupees, which is almost a whole pencil set. The walk is only three minutes longer. I told my friend Parveen, and now we go together. Nobody told me to do it. I just noticed the price and decided a little walking was worth it. - Divya

qa.q: How much cheaper was the notebook at the lane shop?
qa.a: It was ten rupees cheaper, thirty instead of forty.

qa.q: What was Divya thinking when Divya noticed the lower price?
qa.a: Divya was pleased with the discovery and thought a little extra walking was worth the saving.

qa.q: What else could Divya check, and why?
qa.a: Divya could compare pencils and other items, and check the notebooks are the same quality, so the saving is real.

qa.q: How does Harish Uncle see Divya's discovery?
qa.a: Harish Uncle grins and encourages Divya to tell friends, since a careful shopper brings more customers.

grounding: A girl notices the same notebook is cheaper in the lane shop than the school store, and walks a little for the saving.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: waiting a few days before buying [Thinking]
passage: The toy robot in the shop window had a sign: SALE ENDS SUNDAY. Vishal wanted it so badly his palms tingled. "Can we buy it now?" His mother shook her head. "Wait three days. If you still want it, we will go." It was Thursday; Sunday felt far away. On Friday he thought of the robot twice, on Saturday once, mostly while passing the shop. On Sunday morning Amandeep came round with a pack of cricket cards. Vishal ran his eyes over the shiny cards and saw that his pocket money would stretch to four packs. "Not the robot," he told his mother. She smiled.

qa.q: How long did Vishal agree to wait?
qa.a: He agreed to wait three days.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling when he first saw the robot?
qa.a: Eager and longing, since his palms tingled and he wanted to buy it immediately.

qa.q: What other approach could Vishal use to test whether he really wants something, and why?
qa.a: He could write down what else the money could buy and compare, because seeing the choices shows what matters more.

qa.q: How might Vishal's mother feel about the waiting rule?
qa.a: She is hopeful that waiting will help him think, and she smiles when he chooses for himself.

grounding: A boy agrees to wait three days before buying a toy, and by then he prefers to spend on cricket cards.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: copying what a friend buys [Pitfall]
passage: In Class Six, Payal's new gel pen was the talk of the bench: gold clip, smooth ink, ninety rupees. Rishi looked at his own plain pen and felt small. That afternoon he spent nearly all his month's pocket money on the same pen. "Same as yours!" he said. Payal smiled politely. But the pen was heavy and smudged under his left hand, and by the third day his fingers ached. He caught himself sneaking his old pen out of his bag. Sarita Ma'am noticed and asked why. "I wanted it because Payal had it," Rishi mumbled, "not because I liked it."

qa.q: How much did the gel pen cost?
qa.a: It cost ninety rupees.

qa.q: What was Rishi feeling when he looked at his own plain pen?
qa.a: Small and left out, wanting to fit in with the bench.

qa.q: What could Rishi do before buying next time, and why?
qa.a: He could try the item first and ask himself what he needs, so the choice is his own and not a copy.

qa.q: How might Sarita Ma'am see Rishi's answer?
qa.a: Sarita Ma'am probably sees an honest child who has spotted his own reason, and can be gentle about it.

grounding: A child buys the same expensive pen as a friend just to fit in, and later finds he does not like it.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: keeping a small notebook of spending [Action]
passage: In the small-town lane behind the bus stand, Tanuja kept a torn notebook in her school bag. Every rupee she spent went in it: five for peanuts, ten for lemon soda, two for a pencil. At the end of the month she sat on the doorstep and added it up with her tongue between her teeth. "More than half is snacks!" Her cousin Farida peered over. "That's more than the bangles you wanted." The next week Tanuja carried guavas from the tree behind their house and skipped the corner shop. She finished saving for her paints two weeks early.

qa.q: What did most of Tanuja's money go on?
qa.a: More than half of it went on snacks.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when she added up the snacks?
qa.a: Surprised, since she had not realised how much she spent on them.

qa.q: What could Tanuja do if she loses the notebook, and why?
qa.a: She could keep a running total on a calendar at home, so she can still see where the money goes.

qa.q: How does Farida see Tanuja's list?
qa.a: Farida is struck by how the small amounts add up to more than bangles, so the numbers make it real.

grounding: A girl writes down every rupee for a month, sees the snacks add up, swaps to fruit and reaches her goal early.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: goal too big for the time available [Revision]
passage: In Port Louis, Nour counted the coins in his biscuit tin for the third time: seventy rupees. The cycle in the shop cost two thousand. He did the sum with a stub of pencil. At ten rupees a week it would take nearly four years. "Four years?" By then he would be too tall for it. He put the pencil down. So he crossed out CYCLE on his chart and wrote FOOTBALL, three hundred. Then he walked to Uncle Yuki's stall. "Uncle, is there any work I can do on Saturdays? Washing crates?" Uncle Yuki looked at him for a moment. "Start this Saturday."

qa.q: How much did the cycle cost?
qa.a: The cycle cost two thousand rupees.

qa.q: What was Nour feeling when he saw the wait would be nearly four years?
qa.a: Disappointed but realistic, since he put the pencil down and picked a new goal.

qa.q: What other approach could Nour use for the cycle later, and why?
qa.a: He could look for a second-hand cycle or keep saving while earning on Saturdays, so the far goal comes closer.

qa.q: How might Uncle Yuki see Nour's request?
qa.a: Uncle Yuki probably sees a boy with initiative, which is why he says yes after a moment.

grounding: A boy sees that his target is too far away for his allowance, switches to a cheaper goal and asks about earning extra.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: choosing between two wants using needs versus wants [Thinking]
passage: Rekha had exactly one hundred and twenty rupees and a list of everything she wished for. She copied it into two columns: NEED on the left, WANT on the right. A geometry box, ninety rupees, went left, because maths class started Monday and hers was cracked. A puzzle game, one hundred, went right. She tapped her pencil. "The box first. The game can wait for the next pocket money." Alka, her neighbour, looked in. "Buy the game, borrow a compass." "And if you are absent?" Rekha grinned. She bought the box that afternoon and pinned a note on the wall to save for the game.

qa.q: What did Rekha put in the NEED column?
qa.a: She put the geometry box in the NEED column.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling as she sorted the list?
qa.a: Practical and determined, and a little playful, since she grinned at Alka's suggestion.

qa.q: What other way could Rekha handle the game, and why?
qa.a: She could save a small part each week toward it, so the want gets its own plan instead of being forgotten.

qa.q: How might Alka see Rekha's rule?
qa.a: Alka thinks borrowing a compass would do, so Alka may see Rekha's rule as a bit strict.

grounding: A child sorts items into needs and wants, buys the need first and saves for the want.
